1:
The first word they work hardest. Robertson takes it for a passive of the verb to take beforehand, to surprise, to detect; the noun for the offence means a falling aside, a slip in the papyri rather than a wilful sin. Clarke illustrates from natural history: Strabo uses the verb of the rhinoceros contending with the elephant, which tries to rip up its belly with its horn so as not to be caught first by the trunk. Ellicott presses it the opposite way — not merely caught but caught red-handed, in the very act, a special expression chosen to aggravate the detection — then says that whatever the circumstances, one who is truly spiritual will still deal gently. Gill narrows the offence: not schism or heresy, but immorality of life; and he dismisses Grotius, who read it as overtaken before this epistle should reach them, as a very jejune and empty sense.

On the second word they simply agree, and the agreement is worth recording. Henry says the original signifies to set in joint, as a dislocated bone. Clarke calls it a metaphor from a dislocated limb brought back by the hand of a skilful and tender surgeon. Ellicott notes it is used of mending nets, and is also a medical term for setting dislocated limbs. Robertson gives both senses and glosses the agents: the spiritual are the experts in mending souls. Chrysostom reached it first by another route: the apostle says not chastise, nor judge, but set right.

The third phrase divides on grammar. Chrysostom will not let the wording be flattened: not in meekness, but in a spirit of meekness, signifying that this is acceptable to the Spirit, and that to administer correction with mildness is a spiritual gift. Ellicott reaches nearly the same place while denying the stronger reading: spirit here does not mean the Holy Spirit exactly, but such a state of mind as the Spirit produces. Calvin turns it into a test: no rebukes partake of a Christian character which do not breathe the spirit of meekness, and no man is fit to chastise a brother till he has acquired a gentle spirit.

Calvin also draws the boundary the others feel a need of. Reproof, often sharp and severe, must be administered; but while we must not shrink from a faithful testimony against sin, neither must we omit to mix oil with the vinegar. Most men seize on the faults of brethren as an occasion of insulting them; were their pleasure in upbraiding equalled by their desire to produce amendment, they would act otherwise. But the falls here supposed must be distinguished from deep-seated crimes accompanied by obstinate disregard of God’s authority, which must be visited with greater severity — what advantage would gentle treatment gain? Barnes draws the same line as a statement about who can be a Christian: Paul does not speak of restoring one who deliberately forms the plan of sinning, nor suppose such a man could be a Christian.

Luther makes the verse autobiography. He observes that the apostle calls it not error or sin but a fault, and that the word man itself helps to qualify the matter — what is so proper unto man as to fall, to be deceived, and to err? Then the sentence the block turns on: this is a saying full of heavenly comfort, which once in a terrible conflict delivered me from death. From there the polemic: as the Holy Ghost is precise in maintaining the doctrine of faith, so is he mild in forbearing men’s sins — whereas the Pope with all his bishops have been very tyrants and butchers of men’s consciences. Robertson names who the closing warning is for: spiritual experts, preachers especially, for Satan loves a shining mark. Wesley catches the shift in syntax: the plural is beautifully changed into the singular — let each take heed to himself.
2:
What the burdens are is settled first. Gill offers two readings and rules on both: they may be sins — but Christ alone can bear those so as to remove them, and saints bear one another’s not by making satisfaction, which they cannot, nor by conniving, which they must not, but by gently reproving, comforting and forgiving; or they may be the frailties of weak saints, borne by the strong abridging themselves of liberties otherwise lawful. Calvin grounds the duty in nature, which dictates that those who bend under a burden ought to be relieved, then guards it: many abandoned characters would make Christ an accomplice in their crimes, and all would gladly lay on believers the task of bearing their burdens.

Robertson supplies the picture the others assume: the imperative is continuous, keep on bearing, the verb the one used of Jesus bearing his cross; the noun means weight, and the moment is when a man’s load is about to press him down. Clarke gives it an edge: our brother’s infirmity may be his burden, and if we do not choose to help him bear it, let us not reproach him because he is obliged to carry the load. Barnes says the law of Christ would not allow us to reproach the offender or rejoice in his fall, then asks whether this is so among all who bear the Christian name.

On the law of Christ they converge, then diverge. Wesley calls it an uncommon expression: the law of love, the distinguishing mark of Christ’s disciples. Luther calls it a gentle commandment with a great commendation joined to it: Christ, having redeemed us and made us his church, gave no other law but mutual love. Calvin hears an implied contrast with the law of Moses, and takes the Greek verb to convey what is absolutely perfect, so that he who comes nearest with regard to others is yet far distant with respect to God. Ellicott alone stops at the text, preferring the minority reading, ye shall fulfil: its manuscript support is small in quantity but good in quality, and the early versions are almost unanimous for it.

The third verse turns on how general the nothing is. Calvin notices the ambiguity and takes the broader sense: since all men are nothing, he who wishes to appear something deceives himself; and since nothing angers us more than that others should impose upon us, it argues the height of folly that we should willingly impose upon ourselves. Barnes ties it to the first verse: those who feel secure, and think it impossible that they should sin, are not safe. Robertson is blunter — he thinks he is a big number, being nothing at all; he is really zero — and notes that the verb for self-deception appears here for the first time: he leads his own mind astray, deceiving no one else. Ellicott calls it a word perhaps coined by Paul: he puts himself under an hallucination.

Both moralists name a type. Clarke aims at those who suppose themselves to excel all others in piety while they are harsh, censorious and overbearing, and so prove they have not the charity that thinketh no evil; no people are more censorious, he says, than those who pretend to more light and a deeper communion with God — stripped of their high-sounding phraseology, many are like Samson without his hair. Luther aims at the authors of sects: hard-hearted, merciless, despising the weak, requiring all things straitly like severe schoolmasters, persuaded they have the Holy Ghost and cannot err. Had they understood the law of Christ they would say instead, Brother, thou art infected with such a vice and I with another; God hath forgiven me ten thousand talents, and I will forgive thee an hundred pence. Wesley puts it in one line: he alone will bear their burdens who knows himself to be nothing.
4:
The verb sets the standard. Ellicott says it means to test by an objective standard, and is used specially of the assaying of metals. Barnes makes it the word of God, the infallible rule by which we are judged at the last day. Clarke makes it Christ: the only rule for a Christian is the word of Christ, the only pattern his example; he should not compare himself with others, for they are not his standard. Gill turns it into a rule: let a man not concern himself about the works of others but review his own heart, and he will find enough at home without censuring others. Wesley says it briefly: narrowly examine all he is, and all he doeth.

Calvin explains why the command is needed. By comparing ourselves with others, the low opinion we form of them breeds a high opinion of ourselves. It is not what we gain by detracting from others, but what we have without any comparison, that can be regarded as true praise.

Whether the promise of rejoicing is ironic is the one real dispute. Calvin reports the ironic reading — thou flatterest thyself by comparison with others’ faults, but consider who thou art and no praise shall be thine, since no man deserves the smallest portion — and refuses it. The plain sense agrees better with the apostle’s reasoning, and the glorying treated of is that of a good conscience, in which the Lord allows his people to indulge. Ellicott arrives by grammar: his ground of boasting is with reference to himself alone and not his neighbour, his standard absolute and not relative — he will not excuse himself by dwelling on his neighbour’s weaknesses. Barnes adds what such a man is spared: his joys will have their source within, and he will not depend, as the ambitious do, on the favours of a capricious multitude and the breath of popular applause.

The fifth verse looks like a contradiction of the second; Ellicott resolves it on the words. The term for burden here is different, though the meaning is much the same — burden in the one place, load in the other — but the context is quite different: there the Christian bears the burdens of others by sympathising with them, here he bears his own load by answering directly to God. His responsibility cannot be shifted onto others. Robertson softens the lexical point: the word here is old for a ship’s cargo, and Christ calls his own load light while terming the Pharisees’ heavy, so the terms are not always kept distinct — though Paul does distinguish them here.

What the burden is Gill answers two ways: the work God allots a man, called a burden because troublesome to the flesh; or the account he must give of his own actions and not another’s, since a comparison with men more wicked will be no rule of judgment with God. Calvin illustrates the self-deceit judgment will end: a man with one eye, placed among the blind, considers his vision perfect. Clarke states it flatly: the greater offences of another will not excuse thy smaller crimes. Barnes takes the clause for a proverbial saying: nothing so effectually checks ambition, and subdues vanity and the love of applause, as to feel that we are soon to stand at the awful bar of God. Luther reads it as the confirmation of what went before — it is extreme madness to seek glory in another and not in thyself, for in the agony of death it shall nothing profit thee that others have praised thee, since they shall not bear thy burden — then guards it: we are not here in the matter of justification, where nothing availeth but mere grace and forgiveness of sins received by faith alone; he treateth not of the remission of sins, but compareth true works and hypocritical works together.
6:
The verse is evidence about the early church. Robertson notes the verb is late and rare, occurs in the papyri for legal instruction, and that the active joined with the passive shows how early we find paid teachers in the churches. Ellicott agrees there was already an organised system of instruction, teaching being a separate function though its practitioners had not yet formed a separate class. Gill supplies the word: the man taught is, in the original, a catechumen — not a beginner in the first principles but anyone instructed, whether more or less.

Clarke is indignant on the teachers’ behalf. Some believers in Galatia could receive the Christian ministry without contributing to its support, which is both ungrateful and base: we do not expect a schoolmaster to teach our children their alphabet unpaid, and can we suppose it just to sit under the preaching of the gospel and not contribute to the support of the spiritual teacher? Calvin says the same and explains it. It is, and always has been, the disposition of the world freely to bestow on the ministers of Satan every luxury, and hardly to supply godly pastors with necessary food. His explanation is that the ministers were neglected because the word itself was despised, for if the word be truly esteemed its ministers will always receive kind and honourable treatment.

Luther reports changing his mind about the verse. He had marvelled that the apostles so diligently commanded the churches to nourish their teachers, since under the papacy men gave abundantly to goodly temples and to the revenues of those appointed to idolatrous service, until the clergy everywhere held the best grounds; he thought Paul had commanded this in vain, and that men ought rather to be exhorted to withhold their hands. Now he knows the cause. Beforetime, when nothing was taught but errors and wicked doctrine, they had such plenty that out of the patrimony of Peter — who denied that he had silver or gold — the Pope became an emperor and the bishops kings and princes; but now, since the Gospel has been preached, its professors are as rich as sometime Christ and his apostles were.

The threat that follows is read on the word. Barnes says it means properly to turn up the nose in scorn, not to imitate: it refers to the principles of the divine administration, which cannot be treated with contempt or evaded. Robertson gives the same etymology and adds the sting: men do turn up the nose at God, but never without punishment — the thing meant is an evasion of his laws which men think to accomplish and in fact cannot. Wesley compresses it: they attempt to mock him who think to reap otherwise than they sow.

What the deception is Gill and Calvin answer alike. Gill blames false teachers, who to engross all to themselves dissuaded the Galatians from contributing to their pastors, and blames the hearers, whose covetous disposition devised excuses to satisfy their consciences. Calvin names the excuses: one alleges a family to support, another no superfluity to spend in liberality; and while such multitudes withhold their aid, the few who do their duty cannot contribute the necessary support. He rejects them for a reason the world little considers, that this transaction is with God, and answers the fear behind them with the seed: husbandmen wait patiently nine months in expectation of a corruptible harvest, while our minds are not properly affected by the hope of a blessed immortality. Ellicott concedes the language may seem too solemn for an exhortation to liberality, but the apostle has in mind the wider scope he is about to give the subject. Clarke keeps it agricultural: darnel will not produce wheat, nor wheat, darnel. Henry states the principle: our present time is seed time, and in the other world we shall reap as we sow now.
8:
Gill is careful about what sowing to the flesh excludes. Taking due care of the body, and providing necessaries for one’s family, is not sowing to the flesh; the carnal sower pampers his flesh, or makes it his whole study to increase his worldly riches, to the neglect of his own soul, the poor of the church and the ministers of the Gospel. Calvin reaches the same place by grammar, and says he has not left the old translation and Erasmus rashly: the Greek is sowing to his own flesh — to be so devoted to it as to direct all our thoughts to its interests.

Corruption is read at three depths: Barnes takes it by disease, in the grave, and in the world of woe. Robertson keeps it bodily: here it is the decay that follows sins of the flesh, for nature writes in one’s body the penalty of sin, as every doctor knows. Clarke states the whole in a sentence, that you cannot expect to lead a bad life and go to heaven at last, then adds a reading no one else offers: by flesh and Spirit the apostle probably means Judaism and Christianity, circumcision of the flesh being the chief rite of the one and circumcision of the heart by the Spirit of the other.

The promise of everlasting life raises the obvious question, and Luther asks it outright: whether we deserve eternal life by good works. His answer is that it is necessary, after Paul’s example, to exhort the faithful to good works — to exercise their faith by them — for if these follow not faith it is a manifest token that their faith is no true faith. Calvin answers from the other side: though eternal life is a reward, it does not follow that we are justified by works, since God’s undeserved kindness appears in the very act of honouring the works his grace enabled us to perform.

On weariness the readings are practical. Robertson renders it literally — let us not keep on giving in to evil while doing the good — and observes how prone we are to give in and to give out in doing good that becomes prosy or insipid to us. Ellicott prefers faint-hearted, lose heart. Calvin lists what wearies us: many unworthy and ungrateful persons, the vast number of necessitous cases, and our warmth abated by the coolness of other men. Those who do not persevere, he says, resemble indolent husbandmen who leave the work unfinished and neglect to protect the seed from birds, sun and cold. Barnes draws the hardest conclusion: he who becomes a true Christian becomes such for eternity — he has enlisted, never to withdraw.

The last verse turns on opportunity. Barnes quotes Cotton Mather — the opportunity to do good imposes the obligation to do it — and refuses every qualification: not when convenient, not when it will advance a party, not when it may contribute to our fame. Nor is it to be narrowed to our family, our colour, or our own land: if we can benefit a man on the other side of the globe whom we shall never see, still we are to do him good — in this Christianity differs from the narrow and selfish spirit of clanship which prevails all over the world. Wesley turns the urgency round: Satan is quickened in doing hurt by the shortness of the time, and by the same consideration let us be quickened in doing good, to neighbours or strangers, friends or enemies. Luther says it with the Gospel: let us do good while it is day, for when night cometh we can no longer work. On the household of faith, Ellicott argues the domestic sense should be kept though the Greek word had weakened to mean simply belonging to; Robertson gives the plain reason, that they belong to the same family.
11:
The opening clause produces the sharpest philological dispute in the chapter: a long letter, or large letters? Robertson is flat — certainly not how large a letter. He canvasses the guesses — defective eyesight, ill-formed characters, a deliberate placarding of the closing paragraph — and prefers the last, adding from the papyri the contrast between the scribe’s neat hand and the big sprawling hand of the signature. Ellicott says two points are clear: the phrase means with characters of handwriting, not with an epistle, and how large is strictly a matter of size. His own conjecture: the size expresses emphasis and authority, bold incisive strokes exposing the motives of the Judaising faction.

Barnes reports the older reading: Doddridge, Jerome and others held that Paul, a Hebrew unaccustomed to Greek characters, formed them large and crudely, making the handwriting at once a pledge that the epistle was genuine and a proof of special affection. Clarke rejects it with heat: to say the apostle was unskilled in Greek is absurd. he was born in Tarsus, a city which according to Strabo rivalled Athens and Alexandria; and the uncial character then in use is as easily made as the Roman capitals taken from it. So he takes it of the length, as do Gill, Calvin and Wesley — Gill as the prolixity of his writing, an expression of love; Calvin as an argument for careful reading, the greater his toil on their account being the stronger inducement to read it closely; Wesley noting he had not yet written a larger to any church. Henry explains why it does not stop here: the apostle seems to have meant to end it, but such is his concern to recover them that he cannot break off till he has again given the true character of those teachers.

On their motive they agree, then specify differently. Barnes makes it plain fear of persecution: blending Judaism and Christianity, they endeavoured to keep in with both parties. Ellicott supplies the mechanism: what aroused Jewish antagonism was not so much the confession of the Messiahship of Jesus as the declared abolition of the Law of Moses, so by suppressing that side of Christian teaching the Judaisers could obtain toleration for their other tenets. Clarke gives the local colour: the Jewish religion was general in Galatia and respectable, and as then practised had nothing grievous to the old man, who could go through all its observances with little cross-bearing, whereas Christianity was too strict to be popular.

The last verse charges inconsistency, and Barnes presses it: if they were circumcised they were bound to keep the whole law, but no man perfectly observes it, and probably these persons did not even pretend to. Calvin adds a translation note — the old version and Erasmus make it all circumcised persons, but Paul appears to mean teachers only — then charges insincerity: except when it suited their own designs they found themselves at liberty to despise the law. His contemporary parallel is the harshest thing in the chapter: many defend the tyranny of the papal system more from ambition than conscience, courtly apostles attracted by the smell of a kitchen, who regard no decision of the Roman see more than the braying of an ass, but take care to avoid personal risk. Robertson notes the variant — some manuscripts read they who have been circumcised — preferring the present participle as the harder reading. Ellicott says it serves as a blind, that they may point to your mutilated flesh as the sign of their success. Clarke supplies the boast: Behold my converts — glorying not that the people were converted to God, but that they were circumcised. Luther turns it into a paradox: they which were circumcised, in fulfilling the law, fulfil it not, for without the Holy Ghost the law cannot be kept, and the Holy Ghost is not received without Christ.
14:
Ellicott hears the emphasis: the pronoun stands first in the Greek, in contrast to the party of the previous verse — they boast in a mere external, but far be it from me to boast in anything but the cross. He adds that the apostle knows he is putting forward a startling paradox, the cross having been to the Jews a stumbling-block. Calvin presses harder: in that death, so full of disgrace, which God himself has pronounced accursed, he will glory, because he obtains in it perfect happiness — for where man’s highest good exists, there is his glory. Calvin then raises an objection nobody else raises — why not glory in the resurrection? — and answers that in the cross redemption in all its parts is found.

Barnes explains why Paul says it. He had as much occasion for glorying in the flesh as any of them — circumcised, trained accurately in the Jewish law, blameless so far as conformity went — so that by setting his own conduct against theirs he meant to bring the Galatians back to simple dependence on the cross.

The relative pronoun is a genuine crux: since the Greek word for cross is masculine, says Calvin, it may be rendered either by whom or by which, according as we refer it to Christ or the cross. Ellicott prefers the margin, whereby, making the antecedent the cross, since it is the contemplation of a crucified Saviour through which the Christian dies to the world; and by the world he understands the sphere of outward things, with its temptations and its inadequate methods of escape — mere external rites, such as circumcision. Robertson notes the perfect passive, stands crucified, and calls this one of the great sayings of Paul: his old world of Jewish descent is dead to him.

Luther reads the two clauses as a mutual sentence, the sharpest thing in the chapter. The world is crucified to me — that is, I judge the world to be damned; and I am crucified to the world — that is, the world judgeth me to be damned. Thus we crucify and condemn one another: the world judgeth me to be seditious, a pestilent fellow, and an heretic. He then corrects a use of it: the monks dreamed the world was crucified to them when they entered their monasteries, but by this means Christ is crucified and not the world. Clarke says it more mildly — Jewish rites and Gentile vanities are equally insipid to me, and if they despise me, I despise what they trust in — and Wesley most mildly: all the things and persons in it are to me as nothing.

On the new creature Clarke insists on the noun: not a new creature merely, which might be restrained to some new faculty, but a new creation, a total renewal of the whole man — and only the power that made the man at first can new make him. Ellicott notes that in Christ Jesus is omitted by the Vatican manuscript and the best editors, having come in from the parallel earlier in the epistle. On rule he notes the word later gave the phrase Canon of Scripture, having meant originally a carpenter’s rule; Calvin makes the figure architectural, architects employing a model to preserve proper form and just proportions, and concludes that we have no cause to dread the thunders of the Pope if God promises us peace and mercy. Gill makes the rule either justification by Christ’s righteousness or the verse before. Ellicott settles the last clause: the benediction is addressed not to two sets of persons but to one described twice, and means namely; Barnes glosses the Israel of God as the true church, all his true worshippers; and Henry names what is promised: peace with God and conscience, and mercy, the spring and fountain of all other blessings.
17:
What the trouble is they answer differently. Barnes takes it of the molestation Paul had suffered over his call to the apostolic office, his authority having been called in question. Calvin takes it as an exercise of authority: he speaks to restrain his adversaries in language his high rank fully authorised, and though prepared for the church’s sake to encounter difficulties, he will not be interrupted by contradiction — placing himself above all men. Gill agrees it is a requirement, not a request: having stated the doctrine so clearly, he requires that they trouble him no further. Clarke makes it pastoral: end your contentions, return to the pure doctrine of the Gospel, abandon those who are leading you astray, and let me be grieved no longer.

The opening phrase divides them on grammar. Barnes reads it of time, the remainder of my life, and Robertson agrees: the usual accusative means as for the rest, the genitive used here in respect of the remaining time. Calvin denies it: the phrase signifies literally as to the rest, which Erasmus has improperly applied to time. On his reading: this one thing is enough for me, other matters are of no importance, and let no man question me about them.

The marks are agreed to be brands, and Ellicott gives the setting. They are the stigmata, marks inflicted with branding-irons, showing that a slave is attached to a particular temple or deity; branding was applied especially to temple slaves, and those the Galatians knew best would be in the worship of Cybele. His paraphrase is the sharpest sentence here: the branding-irons of Christ have imprinted these upon me, they are my credentials, and I shall produce no others. Robertson adds that slaves bore the names of their owners, that it was sometimes done for soldiers, and that devotees stamped upon themselves the names of the gods they worshipped — Paul gloried in being the slave of Jesus Christ.

Clarke sets out both readings and chooses. The marks may be the scars of wounds received in the ministry, and that he had such scars we may well conceive, knowing he was scourged, stoned and maltreated in many ways. Or they may be the marks impressed on slaves to ascertain whose property they were. He prefers the first: I have suffered already sufficiently, do not add any more to my afflictions. Wesley states the principle briefly — afflictions should not be added to the afflicted — and Gill observes that they might know his faith and practice from his sufferings.

Calvin turns the brand into a decoration, then takes it back. Earthly warfare has its honours, a general holding out to public view a soldier’s bravery; so Christ our leader has his own marks, conferring a high distinction — but these partake of the nature of the cross, and in the sight of the world are disgraceful, the word denoting the brand set on barbarian slaves, fugitives and malefactors. His list is imprisonment, chains, scourging, blows, stoning; and he quotes a Greek expositor who observes that Paul says not I have but I bear, as some trophy or royal symbol, and I deck myself with them. Luther ends in the same key, with a certain indignation: whoso will not follow the Gospel I have taught, let him follow what he will, so he trouble me no more. The marks that be in my body do show well enough whose servant I am — and they are not marks of mine own procuring, but laid upon me against my will by the world and the devil, for no other cause but that I preach Jesus to be Christ. Ellicott closes with two notes: the true text reads simply of Jesus; and though no evidence connects this passage with the stigmata of Francis of Assisi, the word, untranslated in the Latin versions, very probably suggested the idea.
18:
Both who notice the address notice the same thing. Gill says he calls them brethren to testify his affection notwithstanding their instability and the roughness of his treatment of them, and to show his humility in putting them on a level with himself, which the pride of the false teachers would not suffer them to do. Robertson says it shortly: he calls them brethren in spite of the sharp things spoken to them; and the farewell is much briefer than the close of Second Corinthians, though identical with that of Philemon.

On the grace and the spirit they divide the labour. Clarke expands the noun — favour, benevolence, and continual influence of the Lord Jesus — and turns it into a wish: may it live in your heart, change your souls, be conspicuous in your life; and on the Amen, may the prayer I offer for you on earth be registered in heaven. Ellicott adds that the grace of God works especially on the spirit, the highest part of man. Calvin makes the closing preposition the point: the prayer is not only that God may bestow his grace in large measure, but that they may have a proper feeling of it in their hearts, for then only is it truly enjoyed, when it comes to our spirit — so we ought to entreat that God would prepare in our souls a habitation for his grace.

The subscription produces a small textual dispute, and Clarke conducts it with relish. Written from Rome is wanting in the best and most ancient manuscripts; one reads written from Ephesus; some add by the hands of Paul, others by Titus; the Syriac has it written from Rome; the Arabic adds by Titus and Luke; the Vulgate nothing. Little respect, he concludes, is to be paid to these subscriptions: the epistle was written by Paul himself, not Titus or Luke, and there is no evidence it was written from Rome, but rather from Corinth or Ephesus. Ellicott dates it: the subscription as it stands in our Bibles appears first in manuscripts of about the ninth century, though the epistle had been described as written from Rome before that; and he takes the real choice to lie between Ephesus on the one hand and Macedonia or Corinth on the other, the probability somewhat favouring the latter.

Barnes has nothing on the verse but a cross-reference, his block running on into an appended conjecture about the thorn in the flesh, which bears on this chapter more than on its own. The infirmity, on that conjecture, was a chronic ophthalmia, well known in hot climates: it left the apostle blear-eyed and often obliged to wear a shade, made his personal appearance mean, and made writing painful and difficult — so that he generally employed an amanuensis, and regarded it as a great matter when he used his own pen. Whatever is thought of the diagnosis, it supplies the neatest explanation of the large letters seven verses earlier, and of the Galatians having been ready, if possible, to pluck out their own eyes and give them to him.

Luther closes where he began. This is his last farewell, ending the Epistle with the same words wherewith he began: as if he said, I have taught you Christ purely, entreated you, chidden you, and let pass nothing which I thought profitable for you; I can say no more, but that I heartily pray that our Lord Jesus Christ would bless and increase my labour, and govern you with his holy Spirit for ever. Then he adds his own farewell, that the Lord Jesus Christ, our Justifier and Saviour, who gave him grace to expound this Epistle and them to hear it, would preserve and establish both, so that they, daily growing in the knowledge of his grace and in faith unfeigned, might be found unblamable in the day of their redemption.
